description: Solo participant from Coimbatore. I work in data science and built AgniCal, a tool that tests whether NASA's satellite fire counts still track crop burning in India.
summary:
Every winter, smoke from crop burning in Punjab and Haryana reaches Delhi, and India tracks that burning using NASA's satellite fire counts. Those counts fell about 95 percent between 2016 and 2025. I wanted to know if the fires really disappeared, or if farmers simply started burning later in the day, after the satellites had already passed over.

I built AgniCal, a web app that puts NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire records on one scale and tests every Indian state to see if its count can still be trusted. Out of 13 states with enough fires, only Punjab and Haryana show the problem. The count says burning fell 95 percent, but it fell by no more than about 83 percent. Anyone can check their own region.
details:
What it does and how it works? AgniCal is a web app that checks whether NASA's satellite fire counts can still be trusted for crop burning in India. I put MODIS fire detections from Terra and Aqua, and VIIRS detections from Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, for 2003 to 2025 onto one scale. For every state and season it asks one question: is the count still comparable with earlier years? These satellites pass at fixed hours, close to 1:30 pm, but Terra and Aqua have drifted in local time. Together they give several looks at the fire day. In Punjab, the later Aqua pass now sees about four times more fires per Suomi NPP fire than before. Across the border in Pakistan it sees about one times, so satellite drift is not the cause.

Benefits: Out of 13 states with enough fires, only Punjab and Haryana fail the test. A later pass also gives a floor: burning fell no more than about 83 percent, not the 95 percent the count shows. Anyone can check their own region by choosing a state or uploading NASA FIRMS files, right in the browser.

Intended impact: India uses this fire record to judge farm burning and its smoke. If the count quietly stops seeing late burning, policy can look more successful than it is. AgniCal tells people which seasons and regions are still safe to compare.

Tools: Python, pandas, scikit-learn, LightGBM, geopandas and Plotly. The site is a static web app hosted on GitHub Pages. Data: NASA FIRMS active fire archive. Code, under the MIT License: https://github.com/Prithika-97/agnical

How it was creative? Terra and Aqua are normally seen as a flaw in the record. I used their drift as a scanner, since each year they look at the same fires at a different hour. I also built a region checker that works on any place on Earth.

Factors I considered: Satellite drift could fake the whole result, so I ran every test twice: on Punjab and Haryana, and on calm states and Pakistan under the same satellites. I also reported the tests that failed, including one signal I threw out. The limit is that polar satellites can bound the burning hour but cannot measure it. Hourly satellites such as GK-2A and INSAT are the next step.
dataRefs: NASA FIRMS Active Fire Data (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS 375 m: Suomi NPP, NOAA-20, NOAA-21)
projectRefs: LightGBM (model used to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS counts)
pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn and GeoPandas (Python analysis libraries)
